outputs.L1: Hemostatic clips, clip appliers, and applications thereof are provided for ligating bodily organs or tissues in a subject. The clips and clip appliers are structurally configured to conform to varying thicknesses of bodily organs or tissues. Each hemostatic clip includes opposing first and second clip arms connected at a shared elastic, normally open joint portion. The clip arms include outer and inner members having tissue-contacting surfaces and gaps for elastically deforming and/or shifting to apply compression and clamping forces to a bodily organ or tissue. The clip further includes a locking mechanism for securing the clip arms together. Distal and proximal end portions may freely extend from a first arm-joining portion. The clip also includes an interconnecting mechanism for sequentially chaining multiple clips lengthwise. In some embodiments, the clip may include an inner clip arm member with distal and proximal end portions freely extending from a single arm-joining portion. Also disclosed are clip appliers for deploying hemostatic clips, and methods employing the hemostatic clips for ligating bodily organs or tissues.
outputs.L2: Disclosed are hemostatic clips, instruments for applying the clips, and related uses for tying off or closing bodily organs or tissues in a subject. The clips and their applicators are designed to accommodate organs or tissues of varying thicknesses. Each hemostatic clip has opposed first and second arms joined by a common resilient joint that is normally in an open position. The clip arms include inner and outer components with tissue-engaging surfaces and spaces that allow elastic bending and/or displacement, thereby producing compressive and clamping force on the organ or tissue. The clip also has a locking structure that secures the arms together. Distal and proximal end sections may extend freely from a joining portion of the first arm. An interconnection feature may be provided to link multiple clips end-to-end in sequence. In some versions, the clip includes an inner arm member whose distal and proximal ends extend freely from a single arm-joining section. Also described are applicators for placing the hemostatic clips and methods of using the clips to ligate bodily organs or tissues.
outputs.L3:
Hemostatic clips and clip appliers are medical devices designed for ligating bodily organs or tissues in a subject. They may be used to occlude, clamp, or otherwise secure tissue during a surgical or medical procedure, including procedures in which bleeding control or tissue closure is required. The clip applier is configured to deploy one or more hemostatic clips to a target site and to position the clips around the selected tissue or organ portion.

The hemostatic clips and their corresponding appliers are structured to accommodate bodily organs or tissues having different thicknesses. This allows the devices to conform to varying anatomical dimensions and tissue conditions while maintaining effective engagement with the target tissue. By adapting to different tissue profiles, the clips can provide reliable ligation without requiring a single fixed tissue size or shape.

Each hemostatic clip includes a pair of opposing clip arms connected by a shared elastic joint. In an undeployed or resting condition, the elastic joint normally biases the clip arms toward an open configuration. This normally open arrangement facilitates placement of the clip around tissue before the clip is closed. When actuated by the clip applier, the opposing arms move toward one another to clamp the tissue positioned between them.

The clip arms include tissue-contacting surfaces configured to engage the bodily organ or tissue. These surfaces may be shaped, textured, contoured, or otherwise formed to improve contact and retention. The clip arms may also include deformable or shiftable gaps that respond to tissue thickness and compression during closure. As the arms close, the gaps can deform, shift, narrow, or otherwise change configuration, allowing the clip to apply compression and clamping forces to the tissue in a controlled manner. This structural adaptability helps distribute force across the tissue-contacting surfaces and can improve securement of the ligated tissue.

The clips may further include locking mechanisms that secure the opposing clip arms together after closure. Such mechanisms help maintain the clip in a clamped configuration and resist unintended opening or displacement. In addition, the clips may include interconnecting features that allow multiple clips to be joined or chained together lengthwise. These interconnecting mechanisms can permit sequential clip deployment, organized clip storage, or formation of a connected series of clips for use with a compatible clip applier. Overall, the hemostatic clips and clip appliers provide a tissue-ligation system capable of adapting to different tissue thicknesses while applying stable compression and secure clamping forces.
outputs.L4:
Hemostatic clips, clip appliers, and associated methods are used in surgical procedures to ligate, occlude, or secure bodily organs, blood vessels, ducts, or other tissues. These systems generally include one or more clips formed with opposing clip arms that can move from an open configuration to a closed configuration around target tissue. The clip arms may be elastically deformable so that they can flex during application and then apply a controlled compressive force to the tissue once deployed. In many embodiments, the arms include tissue-contacting surfaces shaped to improve grip, distribute pressure, and reduce the likelihood of slippage after the clip has been placed.

A clip may also include a locking structure that secures the arms together after closure. The locking mechanism can be configured to maintain the clip in a clamped state despite tissue movement, changes in tissue thickness, or forces encountered during or after the procedure. Such locking features may include complementary latch elements, hooks, catches, recesses, protrusions, or other mechanical engagement structures positioned on the clip arms. When the clip is compressed by a clip applier, these features engage to hold the clip closed around the tissue.

The tissue-contacting portions of the clip may be designed to accommodate a range of tissue sizes and compressibilities. For example, the inner surfaces of the clip arms may include grooves, ribs, teeth, textured regions, curved profiles, or resilient pads that help maintain stable engagement with the tissue. These features can help provide uniform compression while limiting excessive localized pressure that might cut through or damage the tissue. By allowing the clip arms to deform elastically during application, the clip can adapt to varying tissue thicknesses while still producing a secure ligation.

In some configurations, multiple clips may be connected or arranged in a chain, cartridge, or sequential delivery format. Optional chaining features allow clips to be supplied to a clip applier in an organized manner, enabling repeated deployment during a surgical procedure without requiring manual loading of each individual clip. The chain or cartridge may be configured to separate a single clip from the remaining clips as the applier advances, positions, and closes the selected clip around the target tissue. This can improve procedural efficiency, particularly in minimally invasive or laparoscopic applications where instrument access is limited.

A clip applier used with these clips may include jaws or other actuating elements that receive a clip in an open state and close the clip around tissue when the surgeon operates the handle or control mechanism. The applier may be designed to apply a predetermined closing force, guide the clip arms into proper alignment, and ensure engagement of the locking mechanism. In some embodiments, the applier may also include features for advancing clips from a magazine, separating clips from a chain, verifying proper clip placement, or preventing incomplete deployment.

Methods of using the clipping system may include positioning the open clip around a selected tissue structure, actuating the clip applier to bring the clip arms together, compressing the tissue between the tissue-contacting surfaces, and engaging the locking mechanism to secure the clip in place. Once deployed, the clip maintains controlled compression on the tissue to achieve ligation or occlusion. The elasticity of the clip arms and the geometry of the contacting surfaces allow the system to accommodate differences in tissue thickness and firmness while maintaining a reliable clamping force.

Overall, the hemostatic clip system provides a deployable, secure, and adaptable solution for tissue ligation. By combining elastically deformable clip arms, carefully shaped tissue-contacting surfaces, reliable locking structures, and optional clip-chaining or sequential delivery features, the system can improve the consistency, versatility, and effectiveness of surgical clipping procedures. This makes the technology suitable for a wide range of open, endoscopic, and laparoscopic applications in which controlled compression and dependable tissue clamping are required.
outputs.L5: The hemostatic clip is a small medical device used to control bleeding during surgical and endoscopic procedures. Hemostatic clips are commonly applied to blood vessels or tissue to close the source of bleeding quickly and effectively. The clip is designed to remain securely in place, helping reduce blood loss and support the healing process. These devices are especially useful in minimally invasive procedures, where precision and reliability are essential. The use of a hemostatic clip can improve patient safety and help surgeons manage bleeding with greater confidence.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a patent-style abstract for an invention involving hemostatic clips and clip appliers used to ligate bodily organs or tissues.
counterfactuals.output: A surgical clip applier is provided for applying hemostatic clips to bodily tissue or vessels to effect ligation. The clip applier includes an elongated shaft having a distal end configured to receive and deploy a clip, a handle assembly operatively coupled to the shaft, and a clip-feeding mechanism configured to advance individual clips from a clip supply toward opposing jaw members disposed at the distal end of the shaft. The jaw members are movable between an open position for receiving tissue and a closed position for deforming a clip about the tissue. An actuation mechanism responsive to manipulation of the handle assembly sequentially advances a clip into the jaw members and closes the jaw members to crimp the clip in a controlled manner. In some embodiments, the clip includes legs having tissue-gripping features and a crown portion configured to promote uniform compression and secure retention after deployment. The clip applier may include alignment, locking, or anti-backup features to enhance clip positioning, reduce misfire, and facilitate reliable ligation during open, endoscopic, or laparoscopic procedures.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe an invention for ligating tissue using hemostatic clips and clip appliers, including details about arm structure, elastic joints, freely extending end portions, and methods of use.
counterfactuals.output:
An invention for ligating tissue may include a hemostatic clip and a cooperating clip applier configured to close the clip around a vessel, duct, tubular structure, or other tissue portion to be occluded.

The hemostatic clip can be formed as a generally U-shaped or V-shaped clip body having two opposed clip arms joined at a proximal end by an elastic joint. The clip arms extend distally from the joint toward respective free end portions. In an open, undeformed condition, the arms are spaced apart to receive tissue between them. When compressed by a clip applier, the arms move toward one another to clamp and ligate the tissue.

Each clip arm may include an inner tissue-contacting surface and an outer surface engaged by jaws of the clip applier. The inner surfaces may be substantially smooth, serrated, ridged, grooved, toothed, or otherwise textured to improve retention on tissue and resist slippage after deployment. The arms may be made of metal, polymer, bioabsorbable material, or a composite structure. Suitable materials can include titanium, stainless steel, tantald, tantalum, magnesium alloys, polymeric resins, or absorbable polymers, depending on whether permanent or temporary ligation is desired.

The proximal connection between the two arms may include one or more elastic joints. The elastic joint can be a resilient bend, hinge, web, bridge, loop, spring region, reduced-thickness region, or flexible connector integrally formed with the arms. The elastic joint biases the clip arms toward an open position or allows controlled elastic deformation during closure. In some versions, the joint stores elastic energy as the clip is compressed and contributes to secure clamping after release. In other versions, the joint provides flexibility while the arms undergo plastic deformation to maintain a closed configuration.

The distal ends of the arms may include freely extending end portions. These end portions can project beyond the primary tissue-gripping region and may be shaped to guide tissue into the clip opening, facilitate alignment within the applier jaws, or interlock when the clip is closed. The freely extending end portions may be tapered, curved, hooked, inwardly directed, outwardly flared, blunt, pointed, rounded, or provided with complementary male/female locking features. Because the end portions are free rather than joined to each other, they can move independently as the clip is applied, allowing the clip to conform to tissue of different thicknesses.

In one embodiment, the clip includes a first arm and a second arm connected by two spaced elastic joints. The joints may be positioned at or near a proximal bridge portion, while the distal portions of the arms extend freely. The arms may have a central clamping region between the elastic joint and the free distal end portions. The free distal end portions can initially diverge slightly to ease placement around tissue, and then approach each other during application. A locking structure may be provided near the free ends, such as a latch, detent, notch, barb, recess, hook, or snap-fit feature, to retain the clip in a closed condition.

The clip applier can include an elongate shaft, a handle assembly, and a pair of distal jaws. The jaws are shaped to receive and support the outer surfaces of the clip arms. Actuation of the handle moves the jaws from an open position to a closed position, thereby compressing the clip arms around tissue. The applier may be used in open surgery, laparoscopic surgery, robotic surgery, or endoscopic procedures. For minimally invasive use, the shaft may be dimensioned to pass through a trocar or working channel.

The applier may include a clip cartridge or magazine storing multiple clips. A feeding mechanism can advance individual clips into the jaws. The jaws may include channels, rails, pockets, or grooves that engage the clip arms while leaving the freely extending end portions available to move during closure. The jaw geometry can apply force progressively, first aligning the clip relative to the tissue and then compressing the arms into a closed, tissue-ligating configuration.

A method of using the invention may include loading a hemostatic clip into the jaws of the clip applier, positioning the open clip around tissue to be ligated, and actuating the applier to close the clip. During actuation, the jaws apply compressive force to the arms, the elastic joint bends or flexes, and the freely extending end portions move toward one another. The tissue is captured between the inner surfaces of the arms. The clip is then released from the jaws, leaving the clip secured to the tissue and maintaining hemostasis or occlusion.

Another method may include introducing the applier through a trocar, advancing the distal jaws to a target vessel, placing the vessel between the open clip arms, closing the handle to deform or lock the clip, and withdrawing the applier. The clip may remain in place to seal the vessel before transection. Multiple clips may be applied sequentially to the same vessel or to different tissue structures.

In some embodiments, the elastic joint allows the clip to partially reopen before final locking, permitting repositioning if the surgeon has not fully actuated the applier. In other embodiments, once a threshold closing force is applied, the free end portions lock together and prevent reopening. The combination of resilient arm connection, controlled free-end motion, and applier-guided compression can provide secure ligation while reducing the risk of clip misalignment, tissue cutting, or accidental dislodgement.

Thus, the invention provides a tissue-ligating system including a hemostatic clip with opposed arms, one or more elastic joints, and freely extending distal end portions, together with a clip applier configured to hold, position, close, and deploy the clip around tissue.
